summary.text: A Mersenne prime is a prime number that is one less than a power of two, named after the French friar Marin Mersenne, who studied them in the early 17th century.
They have been studied since antiquity because of their link to perfect numbers: even perfect numbers correspond one-to-one with Mersenne primes.
Many of the largest known primes are Mersenne primes because Mersenne numbers are easier to check for primality; 52 are known as of 2025.

items.prompt: Someone wonders if 2ⁿ − 1 could be a Mersenne prime when n is a composite number. What does the rule about exponents say?

options.label: Yes, any exponent can work
Only if the exponent is even
No, a composite exponent gives a composite number
Only if the exponent is over 100

items.explain: If the exponent is composite, so is the number, so Mersenne primes need a prime exponent.

items.prompt: A student claims that whenever the exponent is prime, one less than two to that power must be prime. What is a counterexample?

options.label: Exponent 7, which gives the number 127
Exponent 5, which gives the number 31
Exponent 3, which gives the number 7
Exponent 11, giving 2¹¹ − 1 = 2047 = 23 × 89

items.explain: The smallest composite Mersenne number with a prime exponent is 2¹¹ − 1 = 2047 = 23 × 89.

items.prompt: Why are so many of the largest known primes Mersenne primes?

options.label: They are easier to check for primality than most numbers of similar size
They are guaranteed to be prime
There are only a few other kinds of primes
They are always the most recently found primes

items.explain: Mersenne numbers are easier to check, aided by the Lucas–Lehmer test, so searches reach very large sizes.

items.prompt: Since antiquity people have studied Mersenne primes because of their close connection to which other kind of number?

options.label: Square numbers
Fibonacci numbers
Twin primes
Perfect numbers

items.explain: The Euclid–Euler theorem gives a one-to-one correspondence between even perfect numbers and Mersenne primes.

items.prompt: Do mathematicians know whether the supply of Mersenne primes eventually runs out?

options.label: Yes, there are only finitely many
No, it is not even known whether there are finitely or infinitely many
Yes, there are infinitely many, proved by Euclid
Yes, the 52 known are all there are

items.explain: It is not even known whether the set of Mersenne primes is finite or infinite.

options.label: More and more often

Less and less often

paragraphs.heading: One below a power of two
paragraphs.text: A Mersenne prime is a prime number that sits one below a power of two. As a formula, it has the shape Mₙ = 2ⁿ − 1 for some integer n. Any number of that shape, prime or not, may be called a Mersenne number. The name honours Marin Mersenne, a French friar of the Minim order who studied these numbers in the early 17th century.

paragraphs.heading: The exponent must be prime
paragraphs.text: There is a quick filter. If n can be split into smaller factors, then 2ⁿ − 1 can be split too, so it cannot be prime. For example, M₄ = 2⁴ − 1 = 15, which is 3 × 5. So every Mersenne prime can be written Mₚ = 2ᵖ − 1 with p itself prime. A prime exponent is not enough, though: 2¹¹ − 1 = 2047 = 23 × 89 is the smallest Mersenne number with a prime exponent that fails. The exponents that do work begin 2, 3, 5, 7, 13, 17, 19, 31, giving the primes 3, 7, 31, 127, 8191 and so on.

paragraphs.heading: The link to perfect numbers
paragraphs.text: These primes have been studied since ancient times because of a tie to perfect numbers. In the 4th century BC, Euclid proved that whenever 2ᵖ − 1 is prime, the number 2ᵖ⁻¹(2ᵖ − 1) is perfect. In the 18th century, Leonhard Euler proved the reverse: every even perfect number has that form. Together these are called the Euclid–Euler theorem, and they pair each even perfect number with exactly one Mersenne prime. Whether any odd perfect numbers exist is still unknown.

paragraphs.heading: Hunting for record primes
paragraphs.text: Mersenne numbers are easier to test for primality than most numbers, so many of the largest known primes are Mersenne primes. The check used is the Lucas–Lehmer primality test, which is simple and efficient and works far more easily on Mersenne numbers than on most others of the same size. Even so, these numbers grow so quickly that the search is hard, and a great deal of computer power has gone into it, much of it now spread across many machines through distributed computing. Since 1997 every new one has been found by the Great Internet Mersenne Prime Search, a project that pools many computers. As of 2025, 52 Mersenne primes are known, and the largest known prime, 2¹³⁶²⁷⁹⁸⁴¹ − 1, is one of them.

paragraphs.heading: Questions still open
paragraphs.text: Many basic questions remain unanswered. No one knows whether there are finitely or infinitely many Mersenne primes. The Lenstra–Pomerance–Wagstaff conjecture predicts infinitely many, with on average about 5.92 primes p of any given number of decimal digits for which Mₚ is prime. The evidence suggests a Mersenne number chosen at random has a far better chance of being prime than a random odd number of similar size, yet the primes thin out as p grows. Eight of the first 11 primes p give a Mersenne prime, but only 43 of the first two million do.

paragraphs.heading: Mersenne's list and modern uses
paragraphs.text: Mersenne's own list matched the primes known in his time up to exponent 19, and his next entry, 31, was right. After that it went largely wrong: he included M₆₇ and M₂₅₇, which are composite, and left out M₆₁, M₈₉ and M₁₀₇, which are prime. Today these numbers also have practical uses. Arithmetic modulo a Mersenne number runs especially efficiently on a binary computer. Mersenne primes also let people find primitive polynomials of very high order, which feed pseudorandom number generators with very long periods, such as the Mersenne twister.
